Who We Are:

A multidisciplinary team from Fortaleza, Brazil blending Physics and AI. Leveraging neurodivergent analytical precision to transform NASA's abandoned Moon-Mars hardware into interactive storytelling.
summary:
"Echoes in the Cosmos" is an interactive, multilingual web experience that gives a voice to the 17 machines NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars. To address the "Abandoned, but Not Forgotten" challenge, we transformed raw NASA/JPL and NSSDCA data into an engaging educational journey for young space enthusiasts.

Users can pick a world, locate a relic on an interactive map, read its "logbook," and test their knowledge through gamified quizzes to earn XP. What makes our project unique is how we humanize telemetry—turning the dry engineering metric that the Opportunity rover was designed for 90 sols but survived 5,111 into an inspiring story of resilience.

By combining verified historical mission data with narrative gamification, we make space exploration accessible and exciting. This matters because it not only preserves the legacy of pioneering missions but actively inspires the next generation of STEM explorers, proving that human curiosity can outlast the harshest environments.
details:
.

Echoes in the Cosmos is an interactive, multilingual (English · Português · Español) web experience built around one question: what happens to a rover when its mission ends? Answering the “Abandoned, but Not Forgotten” challenge, we give a voice to the 17 machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars, turning mission facts from NASA/JPL and NSSDCA into stories that inspire students and young space enthusiasts.

· Live demo: https://echoes-space.vercel.app/

· Presentation: https://echoes-space-guide.vercel.app/

· Source code: https://github.com/valdenlab/echoes-space/

How It Works & Features

Users open the link (no install, no login) and follow the Explorer’s Journey:

  1. Pick a world: Moon or Mars.
  2. Find a relic on the landing-site map and open its fact sheet and logbook.
  3. Explore the cosmic timeline (1967–2022) and the searchable relic archive.
  4. Compare planned vs. actual mission lifetimes.
  5. Take the Mission Challenge quiz to earn XP and badges.

What makes it unique is how we humanize engineering data. The Opportunity rover was designed to work 90 sols and kept going for 5,111 (2004–2018). Each number becomes a story of resilience that a 10-year-old can understand.

Application Screens

SCREENSHOT 1 · Entry Mission
Figure 1. Introduction: the entry screen, where users choose to start with or without sound and begin the mission.

SCREENSHOT 2 · Dashboard
Figure 2. Mission Control dashboard: Moon/Mars selector, live UTC clock, landing-site map and progress counters (relics, years of silence, XP).

SCREENSHOT 3 · Mission logbook
Figure 4. Mission logbook: a relic’s fact sheet with its dramatized first-person story, turning telemetry into narrative.

SCREENSHOT 4 · Mission badges
Figure 3. Trophy room: mission badges unlock as users explore relics and complete the quiz.

Technology Stack & Architecture

A static web app in vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no backend and no accounts: fast, portable and privacy-friendly. Content is layered: a language-neutral data model for the 17 relics, per-language stories and interface text (pt/en/es), core services (i18n, local storage, audio) and ten UI modules (map, timeline, archive, comparison, quiz, badges and more). Media were generated with Python (numpy, Pillow) and ffmpeg, and a validation script keeps the three languages consistent. Progress (XP, relics, badges) stays in the user’s browser. Hosted on Vercel; code on GitHub.

Creative Aspect & Impact

We blend verified mission data with narrative gamification: a Mission Control interface, first-person logbooks (clearly labeled as dramatizations), XP, badges and optional synthesized sound. Our goal is for 1,000 young explorers to earn the “Keeper of Echoes” badge in the first month. 17 relics = 17 stories = 17 doors into STEM. Next steps: classroom guides, more languages and deep-space missions such as Voyager.

AI Use & Data Integrity

Code, text, translations, images, video and audio were created with AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic; Gemini by Google). AI-generated images and videos carry a visible watermark, and the repository documents AI use in AI-DISCLOSURE.md. Illustrations are original, not NASA photographs; no NASA logos are used. The project is educational, not an official NASA product.

projectRefs: Python, the language of the scripts in tools/
NumPy, BSD license, used for procedural image generation
Pillow (PIL), HPND license, used for image composition and the watermark
OpenCV, Apache 2.0 license, used for image and video processing
FFmpeg, LGPL/GPL license, used to generate the videos and write the metadata
Playwright, Apache 2.0 license, used for automated testing
Node.js, MIT license, used in tools, which validates the translations
Web Audio API, used for the ambient sound and synthesized effects
Web Speech API (SpeechSynthesis), used for narration with the browser’s voice
Canvas API, used for the certificate in PNG and PDF
Web App Manifest, used for the PWA
